# Getting started

## Install Java

Ichthyop is a Java program. Therefore, Java is required.

-   Download the most recent version of Java here: <https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/>

-   Install Java

-   Open a `Terminal` or a `Cmd` prompt and type:

```
java -version
```

::: callout-warning
**Java \> 11 is required!**
:::

## Install NetCDF {.smaller}

Ichthyop also need the NetCDF-C library to run.

**Linux**

Open a Terminal and type:

```
sudo apt install netcdf4
```

**Mac Os X**

Open a Terminal and type:

```
sudo port install netcdf4
```

**Windows**

Download the pre-built libraries in [Unidata website](https://docs.unidata.ucar.edu/netcdf-c/current/winbin.html)

::: callout-warning
During the install process, make sure that the location of the library is added to the `PATH`
:::

## Download Ichthyop

-   Create a `ichthyop` folder
-   Go to <https://github.com/ichthyop/ichthyop/releases/latest>
-   Download the `ichthyop-X.Y.Z-jar-with-dependencies.jar` binary file, replacing `X.Y.Z` by the actual Ichthyop version number.
-   Move the `.jar` file in the `ichthyop` folder

## Download hydrographic files

-   Download the hydrographic sample files on the Ichthyop Zenodo Community: <https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10890689>
-   Move the `.zip` file in the `ichthyop` folder
-   Unzip the archive file

## Running Ichthyop

**Windows/Mac Os X**

-   Double-click on the `ichthyop-X.Y.Z-jar-with-dependencies.jar` file.

**Linux/Mac Os X**

-   On the Terminal, navigate to the location of the `ichthyop-X.Y.Z-jar-with-dependencies.jar` file using `cd`
-   Type `java -jar ichthyop-X.Y.Z-jar-with-dependencies.jar &`

# First simulation

In this section, we will get familiar with the use of Ichthyop and the use of the user interface

## Creation new configuration

-   Create a new configuration file by clicking on the `New` button (@fig-new)

![New configuration](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ichthyop/ichthyop/master/doc/console/_static/step1-configure.png){#fig-new fig-align="center" height="200px"}

## Choosing template

-   Select the `Generic` template
- Remame your configuration file (for example, `first_ichthyop_run`
- Click on `Create` (@fig-template)

![Choosing template](img/generic-conf.png){#fig-template fig-align="center" height="600px"}

## Running the simulation

-   Preview the simulation by clicking on the `Preview button` (@fig-prev)

![Preview simulation](img/preview.png){#fig-prev fig-align="center" height="300px"}

-   Run the simulation by clicking on the `Run simulation` button (@fig-run)

![Running simulation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ichthyop/ichthyop/master/doc/console/_static/step2-simulate.png){#fig-run fig-align="center" height="200px"}

## Visualization

-   Visualise the results by clicking on the `Make maps` button (@fig-map)

![Mapping outputs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ichthyop/ichthyop/master/doc/console/_static/step3-mapping.png){#fig-map fig-align="center" height="450"}

You should see larval dispersal off Cape Town in South Africa (@fig-conf1).

![Outputs of the first simulation (advection)](img/conf1.png){#fig-conf1 fig-align="center" height="500"}

# New simulations

In this section, we will learn how to activate/deactivate processes.

::: callout-note
In order to keep track of your different experiments, we advise you to create a dedicated configuration file with a consistent name (for example `roms-noadvection.xml`, `roms-advection-growth.xml`, etc.)
:::

## Exploring configuration file

-   Explore the different processes and parameters contained in the configuration file and their default values (@fig-edit)

![Exploring configuration file](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ichthyop/ichthyop/master/doc/console/_static/edit.png){#fig-edit fig-align="center" height="500"}

## Deactivating advection

-   In the configuration file, go to: `Transport - Advection`

-   Disable advection by clicking on the `Enabled` tick box
-   Save the configuration file by clicking the `Save` button.

::: callout-warning
**Remember to save the configuration file after every change**
:::

-   Run the simulation
-   Draw map
-   **What happens?**

## Playing with advection/diffusion

- Activate horizontal diffusion in a similar way: `Transport - Horizontal dispersion`

-   Make experiments with diffusion only, with both advection/diffusion and compare the results.

::: {#fig-adv-diff-exsp layout-ncol="4"}
![No advection/No diffusion](img/conf2.png){#fig-noadv_nodif}

![Diffusion only](img/conf3.png){#fig-noadv_dif}

![Advection/Diffusion](img/conf4.png){#fig-adv_dif}

![Advection only](img/conf1.png){#fig-adv-nodif}

Results of the different Ichthyop configurations
:::

## Displaying particle depths

-   In the `Mapping` section, choose to represent the `depth` variable, with values -50, -30 and -10 m for minimum, medium and maximum, respectively.
-   Click on `Make maps`
-   What do you see?

## Vertical migration

-   In the configuration file, go to `Biology - Movements - Vertical migration`



-   Read the explanations at the top of the block. Click on `Enabled` and look at the default values of the parameters.

-   Run the simulation with larval vertical migration and display the results. Is there anything wrong?

- Go to `Simulation - Output`


and correct the record frequency to save outputs every three hours. Remember that, as indicated in the console:

$$
N_{freq} = \dfrac{F_{out}}{\Delta t}
$$

with $N_{freq}$ the record frequency parameter, $F_{out}$ the output frequency (**in seconds**) and $\Delta t$ the simulation time-steps (**in seconds**), which is available in the `Simulation - Time` section.

What value should we put for the record frequency to have outputs every 3h?

- Set the new value for the record frequency parameter and re-run the simulation. Visualize the results.

- What do you see now?

- Do vertical movements impact the overall distribution? (@fig-mig2).


::: {#fig-migration layout-ncol="3"}
![](img/vert2.png){#fig-mig1 width="100px"}

![](img/vert3.png){#fig-mig2 width="100px"}

![](img/vert4.png){#fig-mig3 width="100px"}

Different migration configurations. (a) No migration (b) Migration between -10 and -30 m (c) Constant depth (-50 m)
:::

## Growth

-  Deactivate vertical migration and reset the record frequency to 144.

-   Go to `Biology - Growth - Linear Growth`


-   Read the explanations at the top of the block and activate growth
-   Run the simulation and visualise the `length` variable using `Auto range`
-   Now change the dispay and visualise the `stage` variable using `Auto range` for the values and colours.
-   How do you interpret the results?

# Release methods

In this section, we will look at the most commonly used release methods.

## Initial positions in a text file

- Unselect vertical migration and growth.

- Go to `Release - Drifters from text file`



- Enable the block.

- Click on the `New` button inside the `Value` field. Name your file `benguela_drifters.txt` and click on `Save`.

- A window will pop-up. Read the explanation at the beginning of the file. Save the file (do not edit it for the moment)

- Run the simulation.

- Display the particle trajectories by putting `depth` as the display variable.

![Trajectories simulated in Ichthyop and plotted in R](img/drifter-release.png){#fig-drift width="300px"}

## Release zones {#sec-rel-zones}

- In Ichthyop, disable `Release - Drifters from text file`

- Enable `Release - From zones`
- On the `Zone file` section, click on `New`.
- Rename the zone file `benguela_zones.xml` and click on the `Save` button. A new window will open
- Have a look at the Zone editor interface.

- The actual zone file contains one release zone (`Release`) and one destination zone (`Recruitment`). These zones are defined by the geographic coordinates of a polygon, two isobaths (`Bathymetric mask`) and upper and lower depth (`Thickness`).

Preview the simulation to verify that the release zone is properly set (@fig-preview-release).

![Preview of release zone](img/preview-release.png){#fig-preview-release width="300px"}

- What do you have only one zone displayed?

- Run the simulation and visualise trajectories.

- Duplicate the previous release zone (click on the `+` button to add a new zone) by setting different release isobaths:
    -   500m - 1000m
    -   1000m - 2000m

- Rename the zones by double-clicking on the name on the left panel.

- You should now have three differents release zones.

- Preview the release zones (@fig-preview-mulrel).

::: {.callout-caution}

Make sure that all release zones have the same `Thickness` settings (15 m)

:::

![Preview of multiple release zones](img/preview-multiple-release.png){#fig-preview-mulrel width="300px"}

- Run the simulation.
- Display the trajectory as a function of th release zone release zone (@fig-traj-mulrel).
- How do you interpret the results?

![Distribution of larvae as a function of the release zone](img/multiple-release-traj.png){#fig-traj-mulrel width="300px"}

# Destination zones

In this section, we will learn how to use recruitment zones.

## Setting up recruitment zone

- Go to `Biology - Recruitment - In zones`

- Look at the parameters defining recruitment and at the recruitment zone. What is the distinction between a release zone and a recruitment zone?

- Click on the `Edit` button in the `Zone file` parameter section. Select the previously defined zone file (`benguela_zones.xml`).

- Check with `Preview` that the 3 release zones and the destination zone appear (@fig-rel-rec)

![Preview of the three release zones and of the recruitment zone](img/preview-rel-rec.png){#fig-rel-rec width="230px"}

- Run the simulation and look at the trajectories

## Combining with growth

- Reactivate the linear growth module (`Biology - Growth - Linear Growth`)
- In the recruitment section, switch `Recruitment Criterion` to length
- Run the simulation
- Display the trajectories as a function of length (setting the maximum limit to 5 cm)
- What do you see?

## Adding a new zone

- Now duplicate the recruitment zone but setting a bathymetric mask of 200–300 m
- Previsualize the two zones (@fig-mulrel-mulrec)

![Preview with multiple release and recruitment zones](img/fig-mulrel-mulrec.png){#fig-mulrel-mulrec}

- Run the simulation and display the trajectory as a function of length.

# Time management

In this section, we will have a look at some time parameterization.

- Come back to the initial configuration by re-creating a file from the generic template.

## Multiple release events

- Go to `Release - Schedule`
- Set the `Use release schedule` to `True`.
- Add release events as follows:

```
year 1900 month 05 day 05 at 12:00
year 1900 month 05 day 15 at 12:00
```

- What happens?
- Look at the time in the `input/roms-benguela.nc` file. In Python, do this as follows:

```{python}
import xarray as xr
data = xr.open_dataset('input/roms-benguela.nc')
data['scrum_time'].values
```

The above works if the NetCDF file follows the CF convention, i.e. if it contains a `unit` and a `calendar` attribute.

If it does not, you will have numerical values. You need to convert it manually by providing the unit in CF form as follows.

```{python}
import cftime
units = 'seconds since 1900-01-01 00:00'
calendar = 'gregorian'
data = xr.open_dataset('input/roms-benguela.nc', decode_times=False)
cftime.num2date(data['scrum_time'].values, units, calendar)
```

In R, you should be able to see the dates as follows, providing the units as a combination
of arguments to the `as.POSIXct` and `as.difftime` functions.


```r
library(ncdf4)

# Open the NetCDF file
nc <- nc_open("input/roms-benguela.nc")

# Read the time variable
scrum_time <- ncvar_get(nc, "scrum_time")

nc_close(nc)

# Define the origin (equivalent to 'seconds since 1900-01-01 00:00')
origin <- as.POSIXct("1900-01-01 00:00:00", tz = "UTC")

# Convert numeric seconds to datetime (equivalent to cftime.num2date)
dates <- origin + as.difftime(scrum_time, units = "secs")
```

::: {.callout-note}

To check whether the file has these attributes, you can see the file metadata using `ncdump -h` on Linux/Mac or visualize the
file using the [Panoply](https://www.giss.nasa.gov/tools/panoply/download/) software

:::

- Considering the time values of the input file, what was the problem?
- Change the release dates accordingly and re-run the simulation
- Display the trajectory as a function of age
- What do you see?

![Multiple release events](img/multile-release-events.png){height=7cm #fig-multiple-release}

- Go to `Simulation - Time` and set `Particle keep drifting` to `False`.
- Re-run the simulation and see the result as a function of age
- What is the difference with the previous run?

::: {.callout-note}

When using multiple release events, the total number of particles is the number of particles times the number
of events. If 1000 particles in the release stain parameters and 2 events, 2000 particles in total

:::

::: {.callout-warning}

The simulation start date must always be before the first release event. Ichthyop will run from start date to first release event
without doing much (reading forcing files mostly).

:::

## Multiple start date

- Deactivate the release schedule
- Go to `Simulation - Time`
- Activate `Show hidden parameters`
- Select the `Beginning of simulation parameter`
- Click on the `Add value` button.
- Add the following dates

```
year 1900 month 05 day 05 at 12:00
year 1900 month 05 day 10 at 12:00
```

- Run the simulation. Look at the progress bar. What do you see?
- Look at the console. What is the name of the output file?
- What is the different between this setting and the release schedule?

::: {.callout-note}

Serial parameters are used to perform sensity analysis. This can also be done by
writting scripts (in Python or R) that would edit a configuration template
and replace one parameter.

This is usefull if you want to test hundreds of release dates

:::

## Backtracking

Ichthyop allows to to backtracking of particles, in order to determine where the particle comes from. It can be used for example to determine a spawning area.

- Create a new configuration file
- In `Simulation - Time`, set the release date to `year 1900 month 05 day 17 at 12:00`
- Set the direction of simulation to `Backward`
- Go in `Release - From zones` and enable the process.
- Create a new release file as done in @sec-rel-zones
- Remove the release zone by clicking on the `-` button.
- Set the recruitment zone as a release zone.
- Run the simulation and visualize the result.
